item.text: {"question_id":"3B.1","answer":"For 2023, the record shows a substantial formal framework but materially incomplete protection and remedy in practice. The constitutional and statutory framework defined the National Guard as a civil institution grounded in human rights and the rule of law; required personnel not to inflict or tolerate torture, cruel or degrading treatment, or enforced disappearance even under superior orders; required immediate reporting; and provided disciplinary, administrative, and criminal sanctions. The framework also included written, reasoned, proportionate disciplinary measures, hearings, defense rights, appeals, and complaint escalation (BATCH-0055-E003; BATCH-0057-E014; BATCH-0057-E015). The government and oversight bodies also undertook search, identification, truth, complaint-resolution, investigation, and victim-support activities. The National Search Commission updated the registry, created anonymous reporting and identification initiatives, while the CNDH reported resolving 20,667 alleged-violation files in 2023, including resolutions during processing, conciliations, recommendations, referrals, and 371 criminal or administrative complaints; the State Department likewise reported that the government generally took credible steps to identify and punish officials implicated in abuses (BATCH-0004-E003; BATCH-0021-R01-E002; BATCH-0004-E012). These measures establish formal safeguards and some operational response, but not consistently effective protection or remedy. In September 2023, the UN Working Group found arbitrary detention remained widespread. It identified mandatory and prolonged pretrial detention, violence and torture associated with militarized policing, unresolved complaints, deficient detention records, poor detention conditions, incomplete safeguards, and weak follow-up to complaints, while noting reforms, releases, official cooperation, and some positive institutional developments (BATCH-0049-E011). The State Department reported credible allegations of unlawful killings, enforced disappearance, torture, arbitrary detention, harsh detention conditions, and inadequate investigation, while also recording some government efforts to investigate and punish officials (BATCH-0004-E012). The UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances reported unreliable or non-standardized registry updates, inadequate investigations, low conviction rates, and almost absolute impunity, although the National Search Commission’s initiatives remained a qualifying positive (BATCH-0045-E002; BATCH-0045-E003). CNDH records documented serious-violation recommendations involving torture, cruel treatment, arbitrary detention, disappearance, arbitrary force, and deprivation of life; many recommendations had only partial compliance, were unanswered, or were rejected. The CNDH also documented detention-specific risks, including coercive restraints, overcrowding, inadequate medical care, self-government, staffing deficits, and missing specialized torture-investigation units in five states. These findings concern multiple federal, state, municipal, military, and civilian authorities, and many underlying incidents predated 2023; they do not establish personal presidential orders or responsibility for every abuse (BATCH-0021-R01-E008; BATCH-0021-R01-E011). The 2023 Nuevo Laredo cases provide direct period evidence of alleged military killings and contested investigations. UN special procedures reported allegations of scene manipulation, delayed or military-led investigations, intimidation, and no recorded participation by competent civilian authorities, while also recording the president’s statement that investigations had begun and the detention and prosecution of military personnel. The allegations remain expressly non-final (BATCH-0049-E005). Reporting on another Nuevo Laredo incident described video apparently showing soldiers shooting civilians, conflicting forensic interpretations, and the president’s characterization of the event as isolated; it does not establish his direction or knowledge of the alleged killings (BATCH-0010-E004). Ayotzinapa further shows an initially protective investigative design followed by failure to compel military disclosure, investigative withdrawal, and continuing unresolved disappearances; the State Department recorded arrests and investigations but no convictions by November 2023 (BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0004-E012). Overall, the severity is recurring and materially widespread across reported state-abuse and detention problems, but the supplied evidence does not establish systematic state terror or personal command of every incident. López Obrador can be attributed to the security model, National Guard and military-policy choices, institutional responses, and public handling of documented cases, but causal attribution is limited for decentralized or inherited abuses. The evidence supports formal protection and some credible remedial activity coexisting with persistent implementation failures, incomplete accountability, and uncertain remedy effectiveness.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0055-E003","BATCH-0057-E014","BATCH-0057-E015","BATCH-0004-E003","BATCH-0021-R01-E002","BATCH-0004-E012","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0045-E002","BATCH-0045-E003","BATCH-0003-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-R01-E008","BATCH-0021-R01-E011","BATCH-0049-E005","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0004-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The period fit is strongest for 2023 institutional findings; some disappearance, military-pattern, and CNDH recommendation evidence concerns earlier or multi-year events.","Sources identify federal, military, state, municipal, and non-state conduct; they do not establish López Obrador’s personal order, knowledge, or responsibility for every abuse.","Several sources report allegations, preliminary findings, recommendations, or institutional complaints rather than final judicial determinations.","The evidence documents formal safeguards and some investigations or resolutions, but does not establish consistently effective enforcement, completed remedies, or the full national scale of abuse.","The supplied record does not provide a complete target-period account of political imprisonment specifically."] ,"corrections_made":["Added the omitted qualifying evidence of credible government efforts to identify and punish officials, CNDH complaint resolution, referrals, and formal anti-torture safeguards.","Narrowed broad claims about arbitrary detention, torture, disappearance, unlawful killing, and detention conditions to the national or facility-specific scope actually supported by each cited source.","Separated formal legal safeguards from implementation, outcomes, accountability, and remedy effectiveness.","Preserved inherited-period evidence, non-final allegations, decentralized attribution limits, and uncertainty about presidential responsibility and causal scale."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Reopen if final judicial outcomes or civilian-investigation records for the 2023 Nuevo Laredo and Ayotzinapa matters materially change the remedy assessment.","Reopen if evidence clarifies the national prevalence of torture, political imprisonment, or arbitrary detention beyond the reported findings and visited facilities.","Reopen if evidence establishes direct presidential orders, obstruction, or effective corrective action in specific abuse cases."]}
